analysis: Fat is the dominant error (MAPE 37.3%, mean error -17.5%) with a strong negative bias — the model systematically underestimates fat. The worst cases reveal a specific failure mode: the model ignores or drastically underweights fat that is absorbed into coatings, sauces, and cooking media (breaded/fried items, mayo-based sauces, Asian sweet-savory sauces with oil), treating these items as if they were lean or lightly cooked.
hypothesis: Explicitly instructing the model to account for fat absorbed during coating, frying, and emulsified sauces — and to treat visible richness cues (breading, gloss, creaminess) as signals to revise fat upward rather than default to a lean baseline — will reduce the systematic fat underestimation without introducing hardcoded values.

analysis: Fat has the worst MAPE at 39.7% with a strongly bimodal error: the model massively over-estimates fat for low-fat preparations (stir-fry noodles +292%, cabbage soup +180%) while under-estimating for genuinely fatty dishes. The current prompt's 'audit fat upward' rules fire indiscriminately, inflating fat even when visual cues (light broth, minimal oil sheen, baked/steamed items) indicate lean cooking.
hypothesis: Replacing the unconditional 'revise fat upward' bias with a symmetric calibration step — explicitly requiring the model to weigh both over- and under-estimation risk based on the specific visual evidence before finalising fat — will reduce fat MAPE without sacrificing accuracy on genuinely high-fat items.

analysis: Carbs have the worst MAPE (41.8%) with a massive stdev (118.0), and the worst-case examples show a consistent pattern: the model grossly overestimates pasta/carb portions (e.g. predicting 83g, 73g, 59g, 98g, 165g carbs when reality is 7–27g), likely because it treats the entire visible pasta mass as dry-weight equivalent rather than accounting for the ~3× weight increase from cooking. Fat is also severely underestimated when oil-based sauces or cheese are present, suggesting the model defaults to lean/plain nutrient profiles for composite dishes.
hypothesis: Explicitly instructing the model to anchor cooked-starch macros to cooked (not dry) weight, and to treat visible sauces and cheese as calorie-dense fat sources rather than negligible garnishes, will reduce the carb overestimation and fat underestimation that drive the largest errors.

analysis: The dominant error is carbs (MAPE 39.6%), driven almost entirely by cooked pasta being massively overestimated — the model assigns dry-weight carb density (~30g carbs/100g) to cooked-weight portions (~13g carbs/100g cooked), inflating carbs 3–10x. This cascades into kcal overestimation while fat is simultaneously underestimated because sauce/oil contributions are underweighted.
hypothesis: Making the cooked-starch rule the primary, most prominent instruction — and anchoring it with the correct cooked-weight carb density rather than a vague range — will prevent the model from reverting to dry-weight intuitions, which is the single largest source of error.

analysis: Carbs have the worst MAPE (41.5%) with a massive positive bias: in every worst-case recipe the model hallucinates a full restaurant-sized pasta portion when the actual HelloFresh serving is a modest side-dish quantity. The model is also double-counting — in the pasta al forno recipe it lists the same dish twice — suggesting it inflates both portion count and portion size simultaneously.
hypothesis: Forcing the model to anchor portion estimates to the total visible plate volume before distributing grams across components will prevent it from assigning implausibly large individual portions that sum to more food than is actually on the plate.
